f: The boundary practice guide applies to England and Wales.
A legal boundary is an exact imaginary line with no thickness or width.
A legal boundary is rarely identified precisely on the ground or in deeds.
The exact legal boundary is not shown on Ordnance Survey mapping.
A disputed exact boundary can ultimately be determined only by a court or the Land Registration division of the First-tier Tribunal.
A visible fence, wall or hedge may coincide with the legal boundary but need not do so.
A legal boundary may run within, beside or beyond a physical boundary structure.
Living boundary structures such as hedges can move or widen over time.
An Ordnance Survey line records a feature subject to survey limitations at the time.
The precision with which a physical feature can be mapped depends on the accuracy of the underlying survey.
Even modern high-accuracy surveys operate within defined tolerances.
The legal boundary is interpreted from the relevant conveyance or transfer as a whole, including its plan.
If a plan is unclear, extrinsic evidence and historic physical features can be considered.
The parties' subjective intentions, beliefs and assumptions are not the legal test.
The great majority of registered titles show general boundaries.
First registration does not normally involve detailed enquiries into the exact legal boundary.
A title plan reflects a reasonable interpretation of deeds against Ordnance Survey mapping and adjoining registrations.
No standard tolerance, measurement or ratio links a general title-plan boundary to the exact legal boundary.
There is no fixed quantity-of-land limit within the general boundaries rule.
The former fixed-boundary procedure has been superseded by determined-boundary provisions.
A more precise boundary may be pursued through a boundary agreement or a determined-boundary application.
A boundary agreement requires adjoining owners' agreement and a determined-boundary application almost invariably does too.
Fence construction details do not by themselves establish boundary ownership.
A covenant to maintain a boundary feature does not by itself confer ownership.
Boundary ownership or maintenance information is shown only when specifically referred to in lodged deeds.
T marks are a common deed-plan notation concerning boundary structures or maintenance.
A T mark not referred to in the deed text has no special legal force.
The Party Wall etc. Act generally regulates works rather than land ownership.
A boundary beside a natural non-tidal watercourse can move with gradual natural change.
A sudden substantial permanent change does not move the legal boundary under accretion principles.
Man-made changes to a watercourse do not move the legal boundary under accretion principles.
An owners' agreement about accretion or diluvion must be registered to take effect.
Registration with a general boundary leaves the exact legal line undetermined.
Moving title-plan red edging to a more accurate position does not by itself determine the boundary.
Legal boundary presumptions do not apply once a boundary is determined under section 60.
Land adjoining a road may carry a rebuttable presumption of ownership to the road's middle line.
For an artificial hedge-and-ditch feature, the presumed boundary is at the ditch edge furthest from the hedge.
A natural non-tidal stream may carry a rebuttable centre-line boundary presumption.
A lake bed belongs to the surrounding owner when wholly inside one ownership; otherwise no general presumption is stated.
Absent contrary evidence, land adjoining the sea ends at the top of the foreshore.
Foundations or eaves projecting beyond a ground-level line can be included unless contrary evidence exists.
Land generally includes necessary airspace above and subsoil below, subject to exclusions.
A title plan supports the property description in the register.
A title plan identifies the general extent of land in a registered title.
A title plan may show easements, covenants or land removed from the title.
Relating franchises and lordship titles do not have title plans.
A determined boundary records the exact line of the registered estate boundary.
HM Land Registry does not determine where a disputed line should be; the line must first be identified.
The property register of each affected title records that the boundary has been determined.
A filed determined-boundary plan is retained so the exact line can be identified.
Article 4 publication requires a direction dataset and a direction-area dataset.
CSV is an accepted publication format.
GeoJSON is an accepted publication format.
GML is an accepted publication format.
GeoPackage is an accepted publication format.
Data may be placed at one URL or served through OGC WFS or an ArcGIS API.
Uppercase field-name characters are converted to lowercase.
The direction dataset must contain at least one row for every Article 4 direction.
A direction reference must be unique within the provider dataset.
A direction reference must remain stable across updates.
A provider must create a reference when no existing identifier is used.
The name field holds the official name of the Article 4 direction.
A short purpose description is optional.
document-url points to the authoritative order or notice.
documentation-url points to a webpage introducing the document.
Each direction needs a unique documentation URL or anchor fragment.
notes may describe production or interpretation.
start-date is written in YYYY-MM-DD format.
end-date is blank while the direction remains in effect.
entry-date records when the entity was last updated.
If never updated, entry-date is the same as start-date.
The area dataset must contain at least one row for every direction area.
An area reference must be unique within the provider dataset.
An area reference must remain stable across updates.
The area boundary is supplied as a polygon or multipolygon.
All area geometry coordinates must use WGS84.
CSV geometry is encoded as Well-Known Text.
GeoJSON, GML and GeoPackage use their associated native geometry encodings.
UPRN is applicable when the geometry is a building boundary.
Supplying a UPRN also requires address-text.
Supplying address-text also requires a UPRN.
article-4-direction links an area row to the direction reference.
Withdrawn permitted-development rights are separated by semicolons.
Only rights present in the Planning Data permitted-development-right dataset should be used.
The Article 4 specification carries a presumption-to-publish statement when the specification is met.
The publishing webpage should be on the planning authority's official website.
The webpage must link to the data endpoint.
The webpage must summarise what the data covers.
The webpage must state that the data is provided under the Open Government Licence.
The 1m composite DTM covers approximately 99% of England.
The composite spatial resolution is 1 metre.
The DTM is based on the last or only laser return.
Buildings, vegetation and other surface objects are removed to model terrain.
The current composite was produced in 2022.
The composite combines Time Stamped archive and National LIDAR Programme surveys.
Repeated coverage uses the newest, best-resolution survey.
Resampled survey inputs use bilinear interpolation.
The composite includes surveys from 6 June 2000.
The composite includes surveys through 2 April 2022.
Metadata index catalogues identify which survey contributed at a location.
Raster downloads are organised in 5 km OS National Grid tiles.
Elevation values are presented in metres.
The vertical reference is Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
Input surveys have ±15 cm RMSE vertical accuracy.
The dataset states that there are no public access constraints.
Reuse is subject to the Open Government Licence.
The dataset carries an Environment Agency copyright/database-right attribution.
The metadata lists an annual update frequency.
The horizontal coordinate reference system is EPSG:27700.
The published geographic extent begins at latitude 49.943.
The published geographic extent reaches latitude 55.816.
The published geographic extent begins at longitude -6.236.
The published geographic extent reaches longitude 2.072.
A WMS service is listed for the 1m composite DTM.
A WMS is listed for metadata survey index catalogues.
A WFS is listed for metadata survey index catalogues.
A WCS service is listed for raw coverage access.
An OGC API Features service is listed.
The dataset metadata records a creation date of 8 February 2023.
The dataset metadata records a revision date of 15 December 2023.
A related 2m composite DTM is listed.
A related 10m composite DTM is listed.
A related 1m composite DSM is listed.
LIDAR is described as an airborne laser mapping technique.
The lineage notes that hundreds of thousands of measurements can be made each second.
The lineage describes detailed models at resolutions from 25 cm to 2 m.
OS Terrain 50 includes contours, spot heights, breaklines, coastline, lakes, ridges and formlines.
The product is updated annually in July.
Grid and contour products are created from the same source data.
10 km tiles are identified by the south-west National Grid reference.
The grid uses regular 50 m post spacing.
Standard contour polylines use 10 m intervals.
Contour data includes mean high water, mean low water and spot heights.
The product supports wind-direction and line-of-sight modelling.
The product supports analysis of flood risk, soil erosion and pollution.
Exeter is one of the published sample areas.
Newport is one of the published sample areas.
Inverness is one of the published sample areas.
The online download is available without registration.
The tiled national product contains 2,858 tiles.
The tiles are arranged into 55 folders representing 100 km grid squares.
GeoPackage and vector-tile supplies are single national flat files.
Tiled supplies use ZIP compression and are not encrypted.
Contour layers are supplied in GML 3.2.1.
Spot heights are selected from the highest mass point inside each closed contour.
A spot height equal to its enclosing contour height is removed.
Spot-height z values are rounded to zero decimal places.
Contour vector tiles are supplied in one national MBTiles file.
Vector tiles use Web Mercator, EPSG:3857.
